explain.say: The sleepers sit in a deep bed of sharp, crushed stone called ballast. The angular stones lock together so the sleepers cannot slide, yet water drains straight through, and the track can be lifted and realigned.

faq.q: Why are there stones under railway tracks?
faq.a: The stones, called ballast, hold the sleepers firmly in place, spread the train's weight, let rainwater drain away and slow weed growth. They can also be packed back under the sleepers to keep the track level.
asks: What are the rocks on train tracks for?

faq.a: Sleepers, or ties, hold the two rails at exactly the right distance apart, called the gauge, and spread the load from the rails into the ballast. Most new ones are concrete.
asks: Why are there blocks under the rails?

faq.q: Why is ballast sharp and not round?
faq.a: Angular stones interlock like a jigsaw, so they resist sliding. Smooth round pebbles would roll, and the track would shift under passing trains.
asks: Why use crushed stone for ballast?

faq.a: The ground, called the formation, is graded and compacted, usually with a layer of finer sub-ballast on top. A well-drained bed stops the track sinking or pumping up mud.
asks: How is the track bed prepared?

faq.a: Standard gauge is a distance of 1,435 millimetres between the inner edges of the rails. It is used on most of the world's railways.
asks: How far apart are railway rails?

facts: Standard gauge, used on more than half of the world's railways, is 1,435 millimetres between the rails.
Railway ballast is crushed angular stone, chosen because sharp edges interlock and resist movement.

quiz.say: Why is railway ballast made of sharp, crushed stones instead of round pebbles?
quiz.show: Ballast is sharp, not round, because…
quiz.why: Angular edges interlock, holding the sleepers in place while still letting water drain.

wrong.1: Weight is similar; it is the shape that matters.
wrong.2: Looks have nothing to do with it.
